title: Reading Practice 6 - Antarctic Exploration
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice about the history and science of Antarctic expeditions.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: Antarctic Exploration
stimuli.content:
A Antarctica, the coldest, driest, and windiest continent on Earth, remained almost entirely unexplored until the early 20th century. The first confirmed sighting of the Antarctic mainland occurred in 1820, when a Russian expedition led by Fabian von Bellingshausen spotted the ice shelf. However, it was not until the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, roughly 1897 to 1922, that serious attempts were made to penetrate the continent's interior and reach the South Pole.

B The race to the South Pole between Norwegian Roald Amundsen and British Robert Falcon Scott remains one of the most dramatic episodes in exploration history. Amundsen, an experienced polar traveler who relied on dog sleds and Inuit survival techniques, reached the pole on 14 December 1911. Scott, whose expedition relied heavily on man-hauling and motor sledges that quickly broke down, arrived at the pole 34 days later, only to find Amundsen's Norwegian flag already planted there. Tragically, Scott and his four companions all perished on the return journey.

C Modern Antarctic research is governed by the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 by twelve nations and now supported by over fifty countries. The treaty designates Antarctica as a scientific preserve and bans military activity on the continent. Today, dozens of research stations operate year-round, studying everything from climate change and glaciology to astronomy and biology. The ice cores drilled from Antarctic glaciers have provided invaluable records of Earth's climate history.

D Climate change poses a significant threat to Antarctica. The Antarctic Peninsula has warmed by approximately 3 degrees Celsius over the past 50 years, faster than almost any other region on Earth. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet, which contains enough ice to raise global sea levels by approximately 3 metres, is losing mass at an accelerating rate. Understanding these changes and their potential impacts is one of the most pressing challenges facing Antarctic scientists today.
